The forensic technician was then ordered to take photos of the site of the crime, to sketch the site, to collect the casings found at the site, and it was stated that the forensic technician followed through. Then the investigating judge issued an order to the forensic medical expert to draft his opinion and findings about the wounds found on the body. I can say that this was a customary procedure which was applied after the crime had taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Can I just ask you, then, if that was the end of the investigations, or were further prosecutorial steps taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the beginning of the investigation, the initial investigation steps, an on-site investigation and the collection of evidence found on the site. I then issued an order to the police to take further steps, with a view to discovering the perpetrator of that crime, a whole array of operative actions were needed to do that, interviewing people who might have information about the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And if you -- and were such interviews then conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have anything to that effect in the file. I don't know what was done, so I'm not able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And you cannot recall the follow-up of that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall whether the perpetrator of that crime was ever discovered or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have -- in fact, I was about to raise the same problem. I'm not quite clear. Is the only document in this file the on-site investigation? Was it -- is that all the Defence have copied? That's the only thing I'm not clear about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, all these on-site records are a part of documents which Defence received from OTP and there are a number of these records, but all we have is actually these on-site records. So in previous cases, we were able to produce and to -- to -- to have the answer from Mr. Delic about the -- the criminal files. But now what we received from OTP, probably because of war or collection of documents, I don't know what the reason is, only we have these particular on-site records, whereas you rightly pointed out, Judge Harhoff, you asked the witness to maybe refresh his memory, what was the follow-up of all these activities, but, unfortunately, he cannot recall. So that's all we have. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I just wonder whether it's worthwhile, then, going through all of them. But I leave it to you to -- but try, wherever you can, Mr. Pantelic, to elicit from Judge Delic, if he recalls, the end of the stories, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Delic, we'll be talking about the next few on-site investigation protocols. Our numbers 2D03-0248, the following number is 52, 54, 55, and 57. Let's not go through each of them separately. You see if yourself that the records are almost identical, and reflect the onsite inspections on different days, different months, sometimes it is August, September, November, and I believe it would be best for us to draw this line of questioning to an end, but let me just ask you one thing: When you look at all these records - I believe that you studied them last night - and now have you just said to the Judge that you don't recall. Let me ask you just once again. Do you perhaps recall if any of the cases were processed when you were a judge? Did anything happen after the initial stages?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't recall. Most of the case remained unsolved because the perpetrator was never discovered. In most cases, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand, especially when it comes to the few cases of the bodies which were found in the body -- bodies in the river. Even if peacetime that would have present a huge problem. In order to end this line of questioning, I would kindly ask you to tell me, we're talking about the year 1992. To the best of your recollection, were there any other cases which, pursuant to your order, were processed by the police, interviews conducted, evidence collected?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I believe that there were. You could check that in the KPN [as interpreted] log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand. Very well. Now just for the record, since the name of the log-book has not been recorded properly, could you please spell the name of the log-book?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: KTN.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now it's okay. And this is the log-book which is maintained for unknown perpetrators, right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when you analysed a log-book with the prosecutor, you analysed the KTN -- the KT log-book.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the log-book of perpetrators who are known.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now this gives us a totally different picture of your activities, the activities of the prosecutor, the court, and the police in Sanski Most. A lot more cases were processed, and not even to mention the military prosecutor's office and the military procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours -- just for a moment, Mr. Pantelic -- Your Honours, that's absolutely right. We haven't actually got the unknown perpetrators book, but we're actually in the process of getting it. Unfortunately, when collected it was missed [realtime transcript read in error "policed"], and one of the reasons why Mr. Olmsted is in Bosnia to collect that. So it's absolutely right, we don't have the unknown perpetrators book here at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: While we are on the topic, Mr. Delic, would you agree with my position, which is that you, together with the investigating judge, were in charge of the criminal investigation procedure and that the police, as prescribed by the law, was at your disposal, in order to implement your orders, in terms of certain investigative activities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your experience in Sanski Most, and as far as you can recall, did it ever happen that, when you issued an order to the chief of police, Mr. Vrucinic or one of his inspectors, as the competent prosecutor, did any of them ever refuse to carry out that order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that, with them ever refusing to implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to speculate but to speak as a professional. Say, if an inspector refused an order, would you immediately contact his chief, that is to say, Mr. Grucinic on the disobedience?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is only logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The chief of police, Mr. Grucinic, according to our information and according to what Colonel Bosora [phoen] says, was an intelligence officer of the brigade, the 6th Brigade, which was Bosora's brigade. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I put to you that this was said by his commanders, then have you no reason to doubt my words; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, Grucinic as chief of police of Sanski Most, did he submit a criminal report to you or notified you orally about certain overstepping of police authority by any of the police members under him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such notifications or reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. The transcript - and this is obviously important - is recording Mr. Grucinic all the way through. It should be Vrucinic. That's a V. And can I just, while on my feet, say that page 50, line 15, I said "missed" not "policed" as it's written in relation to the log-books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, it's that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you had an interview with the OTP on the 22nd of September, 2007; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I think it took place in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will quote certain portions of the interview and perhaps you can confirm to me that these are correct excerpts. The Prosecutor asked you whether there were certain instances in which the police did not act professionally in the performance of their duties. You responded by saying: "I cannot recall such a specific case." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I ask, please, for page numbers of the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's English version, 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There are differences due to the font size, so B/C/S is 14, I think it's 26 of English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, following their question, which was whether you had any objections to the way the police conducted their investigations, you responded by saying: "I did not. I don't recall having any." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The next portion is when you were asked whether you were satisfied with the police work that was done. You said that you had never had any arguments with them and that they regularly responded to your requests. Next you were asked --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you give the full answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you were asked whether you were happy with the way the police work was done, you said that you never had any conflicts with them and that they respond to your requests. Then you added: "Well, whether they could have done that in a better or poorer way, that is something I could not judge based on my knowledge of their procedures."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Next, the Prosecutor asked you this: In such circumstances, which made the lives of everyone hard, you responded -- you were asked whether they performed their duties to the best of their professional ability, and you responded by saying yes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, while we're on those particular circumstances, do you know, or did you know a person whose nickname was Nunja?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This Nunja person, as far as we know, was some sort of a leader of a certain armed group, which was called Sos [phoen]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what people were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was your personal impression of that group, or to be more specific, were they dangerous, armed? Did they have proneness to crime? How would you describe the group?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rumour had it that they were armed. People were also saying that they committed certain crimes, such as thefts. I remember that, at the beginning of the war, they stopped a truck convoy coming from Kladusa and moving towards Sarajevo. There may have been five or six trucks or more. They simply seized the trucks, and I don't know what happened with the goods that were in them. I know that Nunja was killed in an explosion. He attempted to plant an explosive device --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last portion because your microphone was off. You were telling us about Nunja trying to plant an explosive device under a car.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nunja was killed in trying to plant an explosive device under a motor vehicle, a passenger vehicle. The device detonated in his hands. I am familiar with that, because I attended the scene following the incident. We carried out an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about whether at a certain period of time he placed himself at the disposal of the 6th Krajina Brigade. Did he participate in combat?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any specific information. I was not an army member. Hence, I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that this Nunja and his group, objectively speaking, represented a danger to the people of Sanski Most, and they scared both Serbs, non-Serbs, as well as the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what people were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But -- in your answer to one of the Prosecutor's questions, you said that you issued an indictment against Mrdja, Kokot [phoen] and Bilbija and that the president of the Chamber, Judge Dragica Glusac, issued decision of the first-instance court by which she sentenced them to a term in prison of one year, and that in front of the court building a large group of uniformed men gathered. You also said that these were soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska which were drunk and dangerous, as well as armed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In that case, you submitted an appeal which was decided on positively, and their sentences were increased; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This was a very difficult time for both the judge and the judiciary as a whole in which they had to try members of the Serb community for crimes they had committed in such an atmosphere in which there were several thousand armed people, where there was a threat to one's life, or it posed a danger to perform one's duty duly?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At page 22, and I think in English it is it page 34, when you say about that case, that once your appeal was successful and when they received higher sentences, that a certain Vosko Skoric came to your office who was the president of the war veteran's association in Sanski Most and that he threatened you because you had appealed. He told that you although were not an army member, that he would mobilise you, take you to Mount Grmic to the forest, where he would tie you to a tree and leave you; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, it's not in page -- it's the interview at page 22?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, interview page, yeah, yeah. 30 -- 34, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 22 or 32? I don't want to delay Mr. Pantelic any further, but it would help if he could -- actually, when he is asking questions based on the interview, have the actual page numbers in English and B/C/S ready so I can find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we're missing it in the transcript, the person who came to your office to threaten you was a certain Bosko Skoric; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So there was great insecurity and a lot of pressure was put on the members of the judiciary in the performance of their duties back in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, it wasn't very popular to set up a trial to -- to try Serbs who had committed crimes against non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Therefore, I conclude that basically all of those who participated in the judiciary process by -- and in their various capacities, including the police, which followed your orders, that all such people were put under a certain type of pressure by those armed army members in Sanski Most. Could one conclude that safely?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I wish to comment or to discuss something with you; specifically, I mean Exhibit P123, MFI. This is a letter of the 10th of November 1992 sent by the chief of police Vrucinic to his superior in the CSB in Banja Luka, for the attention of Chief Zupljanin. In the letter he says, on page 1, and we already reviewed some of the cases referred to in this letter, in which he says that between the 23rd of October 1992 until the 8th of November, 1992, there was several incidents. You confirmed to us that many of them were initially processed, such as the incident in which nine Croats in the village of Skrljevita were killed, pre-trial measures were taken. Next we had several other villages, such as Majdan, Miljovan [phoen], so on and so forth; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And as for the first two incidents, this involved certain combat, and as you told my learned friend, Mr. Cvijetic, this probably fell under the competence of the military prosecutor's office; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the second page of that same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Here, in the paragraph on the top, it says that the perpetrators of those acts were mostly soldiers and members of paramilitary units. The circumstances are explained. And the document goes on to say that: "The inspectors of the Sanski Most police in all of the cases carried out on-site inspection and undertook measures and steps prescribed by the law?" Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It does say so, but you can also confirm that this was, indeed, done, because we have discussed that already today.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It says further on, Vrucinic says -- and this is the follow-up of what you had just explained, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. "Some of the perpetrators are known to the police. However, the situation is such that we cannot and it would not be advisable for the security of the police officers and the -- and the enforcement organs to carry out arrests and criminal prosecution of the perpetrators." Would that tally with your assessment that, when thousands of members of that brigade were carrying arms, it was difficult, if not impossible, to carry out the procedure in the same way one would in peacetime; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He says further on, and he states that some soldier and Serb extremists, fighters from the front, that they won't allow prosecution of those who work for the Serbian cause and avenge Serbian victims on battlefields and other parts of the Republika Srpska. Here Vrucinic again explains the circumstances and the atmosphere under which the judiciary and the police officers work in Sanski Most; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the conclusion of his letter Vrucinic says, and I quote: "There is fear of retaliation both in the command and in the army and the prosecution organs as well as in the police, as they feared what might happen to them if they continued processing the crimes in question." Would that be your assessment of the situation as well?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: However, despite what -- of what seems to be a very serious statement you, members of the police, the prosecutor's office, and the judiciary still continued working on discovering the perpetrators of the crimes committed in 1992 in Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the previous page, please, in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Scroll down a little, please. Scroll down -- scroll up, I apologise. I would like the upper right corner displayed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I know it is not very easy for you to see this on the screen, but maybe you can tell us what it says in the right hand writing. It's not very legible, and there is a number, 02, and then it says: Inform the corps commander and the MUP, and then there is a Cyrillic signature, Djukic, and some initials. Can you see that in the right upper corner?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I put it to you that the person or the organ in charge in the CSB of Banja Luka acted pursuant to the document and immediately, given that this was about crimes perpetrated by the army, that he immediately referred this document to the command of the 6th corps. Would that be a fair conclusion on my part?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, how can he answer that? He has no idea what the CSB did. What happened after that. All he can do is look at what's on the document. Anything else is just to ask him to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's enough at this stage, Your Honour, to have answer of this witness. So I rephrase my question, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can then state that it says here in the upper right-hand corner that the command of the corps and the Ministry of Interior should be informed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And for the sake of precision, I would kindly ask our friends from OTP to provide additional translation because it's not correspond to English version that we have here, just to have this handwritten portion on the right top page. In due course. It's not a matter for today. Quite soon. We should have the author of this document, so he will be able to -- to give more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. We have dealt with this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce - just bear with me for a moment - [In English] Sorry, Your Honour, I lost my -- ah, okay. Here it is. Sorry. I don't know if it's admitted as exhibit, but 65 ter document is 610.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's P118 [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] P118.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: P118, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have already commented upon this document. You will remember that this is about the meeting of the coordination board of the Sanski Most municipality on 17th of November, 1991. Under item 1 it is stated that there had been an armed attack on Trnovo and [indiscernible]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The year is 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was this? Do you remember what the attack involved?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that attack. I was present here under item 2 of this document, but when I was present, no discussion took -- took place about any attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In any case, under item 2 in which you participated it was concluded that the perpetrators of the gruesome crime had to be discovered as soon as possible, and measures against possible perpetrators of criminal offences should be taken. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate in the entire course of the meeting. I've already explained that in my conversation with the OTP. I said that certain individuals, and I don't know their names, I don't know the name of the gentleman who had arrived from Zenica. But in any case, he criticised my work, he was wondering why I was not prosecuting perpetrators, and then I had to explain - and I did explain - that we could only prosecute known perpetrators. I explained the procedure to him under the Law on the Criminal Procedure and we had an argument there. I left the meeting. So I really did not stay for the entire duration of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand. Now let's look at page 3 in the same document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 2. Can we go one page further, please. [Microphone not activated] next page, please. Next, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Delic, looks at items 10, 12, 14, and 15. These items speak about orders given to the military and the civilian police forces. Under 12 it says that it is hereby ordered to the officers of the 6th brigade to the military and the civilian police. Under item 14 it says that a conclusion was reached with regard to the command of the brigade, and then that certain groups should be placed under the control of the 6th brigade. My conclusion as I'm analysing this document is that this coordination board or whatever you wanted to call it, it was a municipal body anyway, issued orders to both the military and police with regard to certain activities; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, Mr. Delic, you have also mentioned that before this Trial Chamber and in your interview as well. You had a person working in the court. She was a typist, Mrs. or Ms. Mina Munic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a typist at the court, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mina Munic was Muslim by ethnicity, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since there were armed conflicts going on in Mahala, which was a neighbourhood in Sanski Most, you learned one day that she had been taken to the sports hall. You've already said that to the OTP; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And now, as a prosecutor and as a human being, did you take some steps, did you collect information so as to learn why she had been taken there? She was a friend and a colleague. Did you make any inquiries about her destiny?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I talked to my acquaintances. I inquired about her. There was an armed convict going on in Mahala, and I learned that a large number of individuals from that part of the town had been accommodated in the sports hall. I could only suppose that there was a temporary measure, because of the armed conflict that was going on there, in that part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The transfer of those individuals was part of a military operation to remove them from the area of combat.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assumed that, due to the combat, that's -- the large number of people were accommodated in the sports hall. People from that part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there was some other facilities in Sanski Most where the civilian population was transferred to by the military bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you know about the incident that took place sometime in early July 1992, when a group of Muslims was transported to Manjaca on a truck, and given the heat -- that they suffocated during transport?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume that you learnt that this particular incident had -- had you learned that, that you would have taken measures, as a prosecutor, because when you learned something, you were under the obligation to carry out certain activities.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had learned that, I would have asked from the police to investigate the circumstances, to take measures and actions to discover the possible perpetrators or culprits, and I would do anything that was necessary to do, had I learned about an event of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Was the witness able to have Ms. Munic released?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You heard the question of the Judge. Please answer.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go there. I only received information from some acquaintances that she had spent some time there and that later on they were transported to Velika Kladusa, or Bihac, somewhere there, in an organised fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier the obligation to regularly submit reports. When you, as a municipal prosecutor, draft your periodic reports to the centre in Banja Luka. That's what you did, right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I suppose that you have information about the procedures of the police. They probably also reported to their superior body on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's certainly what they should have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that is also the case with the army. They also have their superior command and they also submit reports along the lines of command.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And did the chief of police, Mr. Vrucinic, ever mention that incident when the group of Muslims practically suffocated in that truck to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about whether or not, later on, after 1992, while there was talk about this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Even when you were district prosecutor in Banja Luka, not even then?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you lived in the centre of Sanski Most, or did you live in the outskirts? Where did you live in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town centre. I live in my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I was at Sanski Most last summer, and I have a rough idea where -- where the centre of town is. So could you tell me how far your apartment was from the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell exactly, but between 500 metres and a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the direction of the bridge?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from my house to the square, the distance is about 500 metres, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And during your stay at Sanski Most in 1992, you personally never heard of any event of the -- exceeding authority and the police station, such as beating up detainees, harassing them, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no particular information about that. I mostly stayed at home, and I only commuted between my house and my workplace. In the evening, there was no electricity, so it was dangerous to move about at night or in the evening. And in the day time, if I wasn't at work, I was mostly at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have information about the demolishing of religious buildings in Sanski Most or the possible perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no information about the perpetrators. But I saw that the mosque in the city was demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there rumours about the possible perpetrators, about a particular group or --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the perpetrator may have been, but fact is that the mosque was demolished by explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your contacts with the police, did you see that the police was also equipped with explosive, or was it another formation that used explosive?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police shouldn't have explosive. The military uses it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your capacity as prosecutor at Sanski Most in 1992, did you have any direct knowledge of civilian population of non-Serb ethnicity being by force expelled from the territory of Sanski Most or otherwise harassed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no such information. But I was often present at on-site investigations where the victims were persons of Muslim or Croat ethnicity, which can be seen in numerous protocols and documents that were presented here, and those people were very scared. They -- they feared for their lives. And I suppose those may have been the most important reasons why entire neighbourhoods requested to be collectively moved out of the Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Under those conditions of huge uncertainty, was -- were there also occasions of a Serb population leaving Sanski Most, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to a large extent. There may have been individuals deserting from the military and taking individual refuge somewhere, but there were no requests for massive removal of Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Speaking about this, tell me whether you had knowledge whether or not in the surroundings of Sanski Most, or indeed, in a significant part of Sanski Most itself, in 1992, there was a constant fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in the summer - it may have been June or July of 1992 - there was armed conflict between the VRS and armed groups, consisting of Muslim individuals in the area of the Prpolje [phoen] and Hrstovo [phoen] villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And from the report from the meeting of the committee, we see that mention made of a number of military operations around those villages in the surroundings of Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, and do correct me if I am, in the first half of 1996, you were municipal prosecutor at the municipal prosecutor's office at Kotor Varos; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1996, when we left as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will not state any percentages now, but practically all Serbs fled Sanski Most once it had been taken by Muslim forces; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the 10th of October, 1995. About 30.000 Serbs collectively left the Sanski Most municipality then, because of the attacks of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Even today it is difficult to give any precise estimates. But if -- as -- very small number of Serbs lives at Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a small number returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you were prosecutor at Kotor Varos, who -- sorry. What was the scope of your authority? What did your work there include?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, we mostly dealt with thefts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm really sorry to interrupt but what's the relevance of what happened in October 1995, let alone 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just give me a minute, you will see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, on the face of it, having regard to the dates in the indictment, the -- the -- these periods are well outside of what is relevant. It's all well and good for you to say give you a moment, but could you indicate for us how this is relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was -- I'm about to finish my cross-examination, so we'll see my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were prosecutor at Kotor Varos in the first half of 1996; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: While you were at Kotor Varos, did you hear of the crime committed somewhere in 1992 in front of the medical clinic at Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you find any evidence, any note, or perhaps a rumour about what happened in front of the medical clinic at Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know absolutely nothing about those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No further question for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic my apologies on behalf of Mr. Olmsted that you are having questions from me and not from him, but unfortunately he had to leave. I want deal with some of the matters you've just been dealing with and then go back to this question of your files. First of all, can I ask you this: If you don't know the answer, don't guess or speculate. Just say you don't know the answer. It's much simpler that way. You were shown, first of all, a document, P118, and you were asked whether it was right from looking at that document as to whether the municipal assembly issued orders to the police and the military, and you said it appeared that way. Do you know from your own knowledge whether the municipal assembly was giving orders to the police or the military?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Next, you were asked about the incident when a number of Muslims who had been transported from Betonirka in Sanski Most to Manjaca died of suffocation in the truck. And you were asked whether you'd heard about it, and if you had, whether you would have investigated. Do you know where Manjaca is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that in the municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Under whose authority would an investigation into deaths in Banja Luka come?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the authority of the basic public prosecutor in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you have had any authority to take part in an investigation in the Banja Luka municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, next, you were asked about your -- the secretary who had worked for you in the court, a Muslim lady, who you had heard had been taken to the sports hall. And you made inquiries and discovered that she may have gone there because the civilian population from Mahala was being moved out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever see her again?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw her after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But after she'd been taken to the sports hall and after the war -- and when you saw her again after the war, did you see her?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the court-house at Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. She went to the sports hall. Then she came back to the court-house, did she?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the war. The woman still works at the court in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, going back to 1992, she goes to the sports hall, you make inquiries. Do you see her between then and -- and until she returned to the court-house after the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there any reason that you could see why she shouldn't return to work at the court-house, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you make any attempts to see her while she was in the sports hall, to find out what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never went to that part of town at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you saw her after the war, did you ask her whether she'd gone voluntarily to the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't speak about those events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So she never explained to you what had -- what had happened to her?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you never asked?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back, if we may, to some of the matters that you were asked about by Mr. Cvijetic. Now, first of all, yesterday were asked about the conditions in Sanski Most in the period of the summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm just trying to find the page of the transcript. It's page 36 of yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were asked - in fact, 35 - you were asked about communication break downs and the like, whether there was enough electricity, and you said: "Towards the end of May and early June, the entire republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina saw the outbreak of conflicts, including Sanski Most." And then you said you couldn't leave the town, there were frequent controls or check-points. Who was manning the controls and check-points?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the army of Republika Srpska in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. So we're not talking about Muslim or Croat check-points there.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if you'd wanted to get a pass, as the prosecutor in Sanski Most, would you have been able to get one?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably would have. I probably would have been issued one, if there had been any reason for me to travel to, say, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And if there'd been a report of a killing or some crime actually outside the town of Sanski Most, would you have been able to attend an on-site investigation, if you had needed to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was necessary to carry out an on-site investigation, then I usually went in a police vehicle. The police would take me and the investigating judge concerned to the scene of crime, to undertake that investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you were asked also about statistics for the solving of crimes, which was page 91 of yesterday's transcript -- page 90 to 91, about the percentage of crimes discovered and detection about 50 per cent in 2007 and 2008. And you were asked: "Did you compare that with European averages?" And you said: "I don't have those statistics?" You were asked for a ballpark figure, would it differ a lot from the percentage that we have. And you said: "I believe the situation is more or less the same." Do you have the faintest idea, Mr. Delic, what European statistics, if they exist, say about what percentage of crimes are solved?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information on European statistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. As I say, if you can just be good enough not to guess or speculate. Now, next, I want to deal with the military versus the civilian court jurisdiction that you were asked about. Under the old Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Criminal Code, did civilian courts have jurisdiction over matters such as crimes against humanity and other crimes related to war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were any such proceedings in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking whether they actually took place, because I agree, it's unlikely given there wasn't a conflict. I'm just asking about the -- the Criminal Code. If you don't know the answer, Mr. Delic, then say so.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, do you know the answer to this: Whether a military or a civilian court had jurisdiction over a crime, was that something that would be decided prior to the trial, by whichever court was seized of the complaint?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So if a complaint was made to a civilian prosecutor, and after the full investigation had been carried out it turned out that it came within military jurisdiction, would the authority still remain with the civilian prosecutor until such time as the court had ruled that it came under military jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such a case, the prosecutor would hand over the case to the military prosecutor's office, if he believed they were the competent authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So would that be before -- would that after the investigating judge had come on -- on the scene, or before?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could take place at any stage of the procedure in -- during which there may be a question of jurisdiction or competence. The organ that believed itself not to be competent to process the case was under an obligation to forward the case to the competent body for which it believed was supposed to be in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in order for -- for example, if a complaint was -- came to your office, for you to decide this came within the competence of the military prosecutor, what information would you need?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to know whether the person reported was an army member, whether that person had been mobilized to an army unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you would have to have a perpetrator, would you? You would have to have an alleged perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if the perpetrator's unknown?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we don't know under whose jurisdiction the case fell. In any case, in such cases, I ordered the police to do their work on discovering the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And, finally, this, on this aspect, if a case which was initially reported to you turned out to come within military court jurisdiction, would those complaints still be recorded in the KT book?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the criminal report was submitted by the police to my prosecutor's office, then, yes, it would be registered in the KT log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if it was then transferred because, after investigation, it was determined that it came within the military court jurisdiction, would that be recorded in the KT book?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to move, as a discrete topic, to the unknown perpetrator cases which will take me a bit more than five minutes. I know it's a bit early, but I wonder if that would be a suitable time to break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.41 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before the witness comes in, Your Honours said you were about going to render your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to say that before you resume your cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- we would do that. And this is on the issue of whether the witness, Dorothea Hanson, should be accepted by the Chamber in this trial as an expert witness. And the decision of the Chamber is that she should be so accepted as an expert. But the -- having been so deemed by the Chamber, it doesn't necessarily follow that her report is accepted as a matter of evidence in its entirety. So once she would have been tendered as a witness, what of her report would remain for the proper consideration of the Chamber would be revealed at the end of the usual process of examination and cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I simply -- is that the end of Your Honours ruling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It was intended to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm really sorry and, it's I'm sure entirely my fault, I don't understand that. The idea was that her report would be put in and she would be asked some supplementary questions, effectively as Dr. Donia was, to highlight some of the aspects of the report. Now you say that it does apply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if I may interrupt you here, Ms. Korner, perhaps I was too economical in my use of words. She comes in and her report is tendered. What is made of the report, because it purports to be the report of an expert and therefore there are a number of - and this goes to the point that the Defence has taken - such issues as they would wish to raise would be -- and this is what I meant where I talk about the ordinary process of examination, and I really should underline cross-examination, would indicate what the Chamber would have to address its mind to as to how much of that report is properly acceptable as being within the confines of her area of expertise. I trust that that assists.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Um, Your Honour, she's either an expert or she's not an expert. If Your Honours feel that some parts of her report deal with areas which are beyond her area of expertise, then I think in all fairness Your Honours should indicate that before we call the witness, as opposed to us guessing in the dark as to what parts of the report you think reflect her expertise and those that do not. So, Your Honours, with the greatest of respect, I don't think we can proceed on this basis. Not without wasting a great deal of time. We have to know exactly in your judgement, whether it's oral or written, it doesn't make any difference, you feel that the reports forth out -- without her expert -- area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would have thought that it would be a more efficient use much time, her report having been put in, and we don't -- unless we assume that the Prosecution tends to rely on her report in its entirety, we expect that the -- we would be guided by the Prosecution as to what of her report, how much of her report they're relying on. But the -- the practical challenge of having to dissect that report, as I understand what you have just said would you propose would, be a -- to my mind, not the most efficient use of the Court's time or counsel's time. We, the -- the reservations which the Defence have made by their motion is something which would be obviously fleshed out in the course of cross-examination, and, at the end of the day, whatever conclusions Ms. Hanson or any other expert would have purported to make would not be something that the Chamber need necessarily take on board. Its conclusions at the end of the day, as with every other witness, are a matter for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I certainly understand it, Your Honour. But the answer to Your Honour's question is, do we rely on her whole report, yes we do. And that's why we've understood from the beginning that the report would go in and we would not have to, as it were, deal, lead the evidence of what's in the report and how she came to those conclusions. All we'd have to do, as we understood the ruling so far in respect of experts, is just flesh it out. Anyhow, I mean, Your Honours, as I say, it's my feeling that the next question is, given Mr. Zecevic's assertion that he proposes to appeal, where does that leave us for, let's say tomorrow afternoon and Thursday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, as I read the rule, the Chamber may decide whether she's an expert or not. On this question, the Chamber has deliberated and ruled. She is qualified as an expert. The next question is what to do then with her report. You will bring it under Rule 94 bis as an expert report and it is then for the Defence to challenge. If by the end of the challenge raised by the Defence, the Chamber finds that there is really nothing of substantive value in this report, just as an example, then, of course, the Chamber has to be free to say that we will not admit the report, or at least not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that's a question of a voir dire then; although, it's a slightly odd way of proceeding because you're the judges both of the voir dire and in the -- and as judges of fact. But the way to deal with that if there was a challenge to an expert or that part of an expert's report that, as to whether or not -- in effect I think Your Honours are saying that she may or may not be an expert at the end of cross-examination. That would be dealt with before the evidence is given in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No. Again, she is admitted as an expert, and this means that she will be allowed to make inferences and to enjoy the normal rights of -- of providing evidence that applies to -- to experts. So you may put questions to her and so may the Defence, which will allow her to make inferences and present them to the Court. But that is her oral evidence. This does not necessarily and certainly not according to the Rule, nor the practice in the Popovic Appeals Chamber decision, does not necessarily imply that her report has to come in as -- as an evidence, or all of it. It remains for the Defence who have already challenged the report in writing, to continue their challenge during her -- during the cross-examination of Mrs. Hanson, and then we will make a ruling at the end of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I hear what Your Honours say on that matter. I will leave it to Mr. Zecevic, if he has anything to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, would it help, to understand the ruling, if I said that in the Trial Chamber's view we don't even have to read the report before deciding whether we accept her as an expert or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Because you're looking at her as Mr. Hannis argued, it's whether she is by nature of her studies and experience qualified to be called an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think that's what we decided, yes, so nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, thank you, Your Honours. So I can take it answer that Your Honours are expecting her to begin her evidence tomorrow, or Thursday, whenever we get to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Can we have the witness [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I just ask, are we going to get a written ruling on this as well, or is this -- the oral ruling is going to be the only ruling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, a written ruling would for the purpose of the appeal, I suppose, and you could probably do that without having a written order so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're not -- I'm not seeking to appeal. I'm just wondering whether there's going be a ruling with reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have given the reasons and unless we are required or asked specifically to provide a written ruling, which we would do, then we would not -- we would -- we would given written ruling if we are so asked or required by the parties, but if none of the parties wish to see a written ruling, we would prefer not to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, I'm sorry, you've been kept waiting slightly. There's one other matter that I should have ask you before I look at the unknown perpetrator cases with you again. And that's this: You told Mr. Cvijetic yesterday that - forgive me, on the page - yes. He put it to you yesterday at page 73 that he was going to ask you whether you agreed with him and he said: "I honestly admit at the moment I can't compare that with your log-book. But in principle, do you agree with me that most of the criminal reports and crimes, as well as perpetrators, were processed by the military organs; is that correct?" And your reply was: "It's very difficult to compare without the data, but it does appear that they were dealing with a number of cases." Now, it may be clear from that answer, but are you able to offer any proper comparison with the number of cases that were dealt with by your office and the numbers which were processed by the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now next, as I say, the unknown perpetrator cases, which you have been shown a number of these by the Defence. And you haven't had an opportunity - because we haven't got the book at the moment - to look at the book that contains the records of these cases. Can you just confirm - I think you have - that there is a book that contains the list of the complaints, where the perpetrators were unknown?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the basic prosecutor's office in Sanski Most, there was a register with all the criminal reports against unknown perpetrators. That register, as well as the other registers after the 10th of October, 1995 -- or, rather, before that date, they were on -- in the office of the prosecutor. After that date, I have no idea as to the fate of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. That's our responsibility. All right. Looking through the case files, as you have with -- as you did last night and you have with Mr. Pantelic largely this morning, is this right, they typically consist from what we've seen of an on-site investigation report; is that right? I'm going to list the documents. I just want to check that with you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then there's a letter from you, instructing the police to conduct an investigation and to file a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, finally, a criminal report by the police which says they couldn't identify the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now if there was a thorough investigation carried out, what other documents would be expect to find in these files?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect to find Official Notes on any interviews conducted with potential witnesses or people who may have any type of information in relation to the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about forensic evidence? Would you expect to find that in these files, even though they were unknown perpetrators? Scientific evidence.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were such pre-trial measures, such as searches of apartments or premises, and in case some weapons were seized for which it was suspected may have been used in the commission of the crime, in that case, forensic testing would be done, in order to compare the spent cartridges found on the scene with additional cartridges fired from that weapon. In that case, that could be used as evidence to prove that the person to whom the weapon belonged is actually the perpetrator of the crime, in case that those cartridges exhibited the same characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So it would include -- so you'd expect, would you, that the file would contain a list of items taken from the scene, such as spent cartridges?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about photographs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, photographs as well, taken during an on-site investigation, say, pictures of the corpse and the area where the incident took place. That would also be used as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's even in a case where the perpetrator is not known.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, is the job of the police done once they file an unknown perpetrator criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. The police work is not done by that. If there is a statute of limitations for that particular crime, they are duty-bound do keep searching for the perpetrators of that crime until such date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if a perpetrator was discovered for something that had been originally logged in the unknown perpetrators' book, would it be transferred from that book to the known perpetrators' book?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the log-book of unknown perpetrators, it would be stated that the case was resolved; and in the log-book of known perpetrators, there would be a reference provided, pointing back to the log-book of unknown perpetrators. There would be a link and there would be a statement showing that that particular case is closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now if you can't answer this, do say so straight away. Do you know how many of the unknown perpetrator cases of which we've looked at, presumably only some in detail, were actually resolved either in 1992 or later, whilst you were still at Sanski Most? In other words, perpetrators were identified.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the figure may have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, were any?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. But without being able to look at the log-books, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned that conditions were bad in Sanski Most between June and -- and August -- until between June and August of 1992. Did conditions improve after that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somewhat, perhaps. But throughout 1992 and 1993, generally speaking, the situation was bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, can I ask you this: After August of 1992, are you aware of the police going back to try and solve any of these unknown perpetrator cases, where the victims were either Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that data. I presume that they worked on those cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, don't presume. If you don't have the data, you don't have the data. All right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now I just want to ask you a couple of questions about three of the files, in fact five in all, that you were asked about in cross-examination. The first one is the one that was marked 2D03-0094. And you will -- I think you have got the file in front of you, still, have you? I don't know where it is it in your file but ... I don't know how we're going to get this up on the screen because I don't know how it was being brought up ... Was yours -- sorry? Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, can you find -- it's the one -- it should be the date of the -- the folder, or the file, is the 23rd of February, 1993. I don't know if those are in order. So if you've got a file there. I think they're in date order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] oh, I see. Index tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you find that there, sir, in your file? The thing you got there.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the criminal report on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but I need you to have the whole thing open, the whole file, please, that you were given. It's one that has a photograph in it of a -- an identity card belonging to somebody called Nedjeljko something or other. All right. Just confirm: This is an unknown perpetrator, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does it contain, however, some kind of a record of a confession made in 1993? I'm going to have ask you to just tell us very -- by having another look at it; and, if so, by whom.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attached to the criminal report there was a -- an Official Note of an interview that was done with the Simas Salkic [phoen] who was the spouse of the deceased.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, a confession by a perpetrator. Sorry, sir, it's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this Official Note with the confession is concerned, I cannot remember now that it was received by my office, and here I see that the signature of the authorised official is missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But sorry, sir, what I want to know is has somebody allegedly confessed to this crime?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I have no knowledge of this at this moment. If I could take a look at the log-books from 1993, I would be able to establish whether these three persons mentioned are, indeed, entered there as perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, okay. I think the best thing, sir, I won't trouble you and we'll arrange to get this translated. I think that's probably the simplest way of dealing with it. All right. Next, can I ask you to look, please, at 2D03-0107, which is the next document in your file, I hope, which is a report, 9th of the 12th 1992, with the number on top, 00482378. Is that the next document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. You were asked about this, and you said that somebody called -- there was mention of someone called Salko in there, a Muslim name, and Mr. Pantelic put it to you that somebody pretended to be a Muslim when committing this crime. Is there anything to suggest that he pretended to be a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is the statement given by the mother of the victim. She gave a statement to the police inspector and says there that the person in question purportedly stated that name to her as being his own name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But when you say "purported," do you mean she saying he clearly wasn't a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't know who that person was and, therefore, cannot speak about ethnicity. But the statement which is part of the file shows that Marija Pavicic stated that that person had said to Pero's wife Branka that Salko was the one who had killed Pero. And since that person has not been found, I don't know his ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, thank you. And then could you move, please, to 112. And all I want to ask you about this, is you were asked -- in this case, this was several suspects and you were asked was this forwarded to the military. And you said: "It's possible that the police forwarded this case to the military." Do you actually know one way or another?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And, finally, 0149 to 2D03-0149 which is the -- has got the date on the front of the 15th of March 1993, and it's the one where we had a couple of pages translated. And I just wanted to see if I understand this. Is the suspect a reserve police officer in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. It's --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it. Yes, in my letter dated 8 December 1992, sent to the SJB, Sanski Most, mention is made of one Zoran Miladinovic, who was a reserve police officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Sorry. In which case, if he's the suspect, why is it an unknown perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't my impression that he was a suspect. But he was the person who, on that day, had contact with the person whose body was later discovered. That is why I demanded that the police interview him, in order to elicit possible evidence with regard to the events of that day or the movements of the victim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And does the -- does the file reveal whether the police did anything?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The criminal report, which was filed against an unknown perpetrator dated 15 March 1993, shows that enclosed with it, there is a -- the note of an interview conducted with Zoran Miladinovic and there are five or six more persons. But I don't have the content of that note or -- here, so I don't know what the persons in question said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this file doesn't show any further information about this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to ask you about -- sorry, just one other, and that's at Kajtez case which you were asked about by both Mr. Pantelic and in more detail by Mr. Cvijetic. That was a notorious case, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Those murders that took place at Skrljevita? Were you aware of what happened in this case further on? I'm going to ask you to look at document, please, for a moment, which is 65 ter 2063. Now, because these men were in fact part of the 6th Krajina Brigade it was transferred to the military court. Were you aware that when they appeared on the 2nd of January 1993, they were released from custody?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But I appreciate you won't have seen the document. It's just a reminder, or you may not. But I'm just asking you it because of -- this was so notorious, you heard that these men had been released from custody by the military court?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear of that. But later I learned that before the district court in Banja Luka, last year or so, these two persons, Kajtez and Maksimovic stood trial. And as far as I know, they were acquitted by the court. And I am surprised by that, because I had the opportunity to speak to my fellow prosecutor who worked with me for the district prosecutor's office in Banja Luka and who was in charge of this case. She even asked me some questions. She wanted me to clarify some circumstances because I was present at the on-site investigation. And in speaking to her, I learned that Kajtez admitted to having committed the crime several times but he was also -- but there was also an eye-witness who survived by chance, but allegedly that person was unable to identify Kajtez as the one who had shot at him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that was going to be my last question in the series: Were you aware - and obviously you were because you'd done the on-site investigation - that these men only came to trial last year in Banja Luka. Can I just ask you one other thing about this whole case. Could you have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please, Exhibit 65 ter 2065.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This is a document, 21st of September, 1993, addressed to the military court on behalf of Kajtez, setting out his military career and then his background. Apparently in the Second World War, his relatives were killed by the -- it's called the Ustasha. And asking the court to take this into account when he was back in custody and then released again and so on. Now, were you aware that the SDS, in fact President Vrkes, had written asking for leniency for this man?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally -- thank you, Mr. Delic, that's all I'm going to ask you about the unknown perps . Just one other thing about the crimes on the indictment. Just so that we quite understand it, you asked by Mr. Olmstead about this, you were given a copy of the indictment and asked to look at the allegations of crime that are reflected in this indictment which relate to Sanski Most; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
