utterances.text: And today -- I'm sorry, yesterday, again, Mr. Cvijetic said to you: "Is there a possibility that the acts alleged in the indictment were perpetrated who fall under three criteria: That they were military personnel; that the acts were committed in the area of responsibility or in the area of deployment of military unit; and, thirdly, that the crimes were of such a nature that they had to be prosecuted by the military prosecutor's office, and I'm talking about war crimes, armed rebellion," and so on, and you said is that a possibility. Well, we've already been through that -- the areas of responsibility. But, can we just for one moment remind ourselves of what's in the indictment, when I find my own copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I had it a moment ago and, of course, I've left it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One of the allegations against the two defendants in the indictment is that prisoners kept in the SJB building were beaten during and after interrogation with rifle butts, electric cables, poles, feet, and fists. In some cases the beatings were so sever as to result in serious injury, permanent disfigurement, and death. Have you any reason to believe that those who were in charge in the SJB were military personnel as opposed to police personnel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to believe that they were military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In the garage attached to the Betonirka factory, it's right, isn't it, that's right next door to the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Beside the police station, there was a concrete factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Numerous detainees, forced into 3 by 5 metre cells with no ventilation, no toilet, no beds, no running water, eat tainted food, forced to line up, beaten, et cetera, et cetera. Any reason to think that that had anything to do with the military, that particular prison or place of detention?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours I have a complaint if I may. I think that it would be fair to ask the witness first whether he has knowledge at all about persons being imprisoned at Betonirka and whether he knows anything at all about Betonirka because like this we're not sure whether he knows anything about that. Apart from that, I don't think that I asked the witness questions about this topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, first, Your Honour, to deal with the last part of the objection first, I read out the actual question that was asked. Is there a possibility that these acts alleged in the indictment ... et cetera, so, clearly a question asked. As regards the second that, of course, is the point that no -- none of these matters were ever the subject of complaints to his office and therefore that's why I'm trying to show that the question asked bears no relevance to those -- the allegations in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As I understand the first part of Mr. Cvijetic's objection, it is that there was -- in my words, not his, in fairness to the witness, there should have been a preliminary question before you asked the question you asked, dealing specifically with this site. And it seems to me there is some merit in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. Delic, that people who had been -- not sure what the right word is. I won't say arrested but detained were being kept not only in the SJB but in the factory garage that was next to the SJB?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You never heard that at all, from anybody?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I think that in this context this question should be asked of the witness, whether he knew of any persons detained at the SJB building. So questions about that building, no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know that people had been detained by the police, the Serb police in Sanski Most, in the SJB building?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So at no stage were you at the public prosecutor ever asked to process anybody that had been taken to and detained in the SJB building or the factory garage?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I received no criminal report against these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You did, however, know, didn't you, that people -- because you told us that people were being held in the Hasan Kikic sports hall?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was speaking about the sports hall in the Narodni Front neighbourhood, and the Hasan Kikic is an elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you've never heard of anybody being detained there either?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever wonder what had happened to Judge Adil Draganovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he spent sometime at Manjaca, but I don't know how he got there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, but after he was taken from the court-house, do you know where he was taken to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that we mentioned Mr. Draganovic in our cross-examination. Maybe with next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't know, in the future Adil Draganovic will come.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to explore what he is saying about knowing who had been taken to these various places, and he mentioned Judge Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know where he had gone after he'd been taken from the court-house?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that he was taken away from the court-house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's my fault then. I thought you said earlier on that somebody, Mr. Vrkes and other people arrived and that the various Muslims and Croats were taken. Is that right, or is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, nobody took anybody away. But there was a meeting when Vlato Vrkes announced that I had been appointed prosecutor, but nobody was taken away on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the mosques then, shall we, that are on the indictment. The -- well, we know, we've been told that every mosque in Sanski Most, I think, was destroyed during this period. Would you agree with that? And I mean the municipality, not just in the town.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the mosque in down-town Sanski Most was destroyed, and I saw that in some villages exclusively populated by Muslims, to which we went to conduct on-site investigation there, that maybe two or three more mosques were destroyed. But I don't know exactly how many mosques there were in the municipalities or how many were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You did know about the one in Mahala, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was any criminal -- destroying a mosque, would you -- do you agree, is a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is this right, the Catholic church? Was there a Catholic church in Sanski Most Town?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that also destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any criminal reports from the police on the destruction of the mosque or the Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just so we finally understand that, there were -- is this right: Only seven cases recorded in the book in the whole of 1992 where the allegation was that the Serbs -- a Serb had perpetrated a crime against a non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not for all of 1992. That's only the period from the end of May --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- up until -- that's what we found in the log-book. That's the number of persons reported in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honour, just for the record, I would kindly ask my learned friend Ms. Korner mentioned something during re-direct of this witness along the lines that court in Banja Luka only last year finalized the criminal procedures against Kajtez and the others. Please, in future for two simple reasons avoid your ironic remarks because we are short in time here. We have to be very efficient. And number two, even now it is a fact of common knowledge that even now after the Second World War still we have certain proceedings, not to mention this particular Tribunal, or Rwanda Tribunal, or even Federal Tribunal in Bosnia, so, please, it would be fair not to -- to have this kind of ironic remarks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. And, of course, --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic and I -- I only say that the Chamber expects that all counsel would conduct themselves appropriately and control their inclinations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, we thank you very much for coming to assist the Tribunal, and we wish you a safe passage back to your home. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness will be called by Mr. Demirdjian, who I should have said joined us at the afternoon session. We haven't finished with Sanski Most by a long chalk. But because of the witness problems, we're moving to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The next witness is Witness ST-34, Mr. Isak Gasi, from the municipality of Brcko. He has no protective measures and I expect to be one hour with him. In relation to his evidence, I could quickly introduce the fact that he will be dealing with killings in Schedule B of the indictment, killings at the Luka camp at the SJB building, unlawful detention, torture, cruel treatment, and inhumane acts, as Schedule C and D. Again at the SJB building at Luka camp. And, finally, Schedule F, attacks on non-Serb parts of the town of Brcko; and Schedule G, takeover of power in the municipality of Brcko. That would be the introduction, and we may introduce the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. What is your name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Isak Gasi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Bosnia before the war, I used to be to an electrician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And in what town do you reside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the war it was Brcko; whereas now, I reside in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Your date of birth is when, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 5th of April, 1957.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The 5th of May, 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Brcko, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Bosnian Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you given evidence in these proceedings on a previous occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have. Three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so you would be well aware of the procedure, whereby the side calling you, in this case, the Prosecution, would have questions for you, followed by the lawyers representing the -- each of the two accused, and after re-examination by the Prosecution, the Chamber itself may have some questions of you. Thank you. Thank you for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, is it correct to say that you testified in the past in the Tadic case, the Milosevic case, and the Krajisnik case?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. In all three cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The last time you testified in the Krajisnik case, that was on the 4th and 5th of February 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that is the testimony we're going to be relying upon for the purposes of this 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gasi, when you arrived here a few days ago were you provided with your testimony, the one that you gave in the Krajisnik case?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. You gave it to me to prepare myself. I went through the whole of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you provided your evidence back in 2004, did you answer the questions as honestly and as accurately as could?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. To the extent of my knowledge and about things that I was certain of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions about the same topics, would you provide the same answers before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I probably would.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that 65 ter 1021 and 1022 be admitted in evidence, and these are the transcripts of his testimony on the 4th and 5th of February 2004 in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P125 and P126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, I will ask you a number of questions dealing with the events in 1991 and 1992, starting with the municipality of Brcko itself. Just for the purposes of the Court, it is correct to say that Brcko is a municipality in the north-east part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, bordering with Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony in Krajisnik - and for Your Honours at pages 407 - you explained that during the early months of 1992 tensions were rising and that you attended a session of the Brcko Municipal Assembly during which you heard discussions about the division of the town of Brcko. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It may have been April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you recall roughly which part of April this was?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: It is possible that it was the second week of April. Although I may be mistaken as well. I think it was around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us who attended this session of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: In attendance were those people reflecting the results of the first multi-party elections in Brcko; that is to say, the representatives of the three ethnic community and their parties, the HDZ, SDS, and SDA. There were also certain representatives from the SDP, which was the Former League of Communists party. Among other things, there was discussion on any future events in Brcko and how to calm down the situation. It was mentioned that a lot of people in Brcko listened to different types of rumours, semi-truths, and people were basically trying to gain more information during such sessions. I was not an elective deputy, though, I was only there with a friend of mine who was a journalist. There was speeches made by delegates of different political parties. I was rather impressed seeing people from the SDS jumping up, taking up of the floor. There was a friend of mine who was a member of the executive board in the local SDS took the floor. I think his name was Listanic [as interpreted], and it was he who asked for a tripartite division of the Brcko territory on behalf of his party. He wanted a part for the Muslims, another part for the Croats, and a third part for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. In the transcript at line 22, page 102, it reads "Listanic." Was that the last name you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Ristanic, Djordje Ristanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And it is correct that he said, and this is in the transcripts at page 407 in your Krajisnik testimony, he said the words: "We will divide it or we will have problems."

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. He said that unless we reach an agreement on the division of the Brcko municipality into three parts there would be problems which will probably come about after the 4th of May. This was almost an ultimatum, a threat. As far as I could gather at the time, the other parties disagreed with it. That is to say, the Muslim party, and the Croatian party, as well as the former Communists. They simply rejected any discussion of the division of the Brcko municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, did they explain during this meeting which parts of the town the SDS wanted to be part of the Serbian Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, based on the maps of the town of Brcko, what they wanted to have was most of the industrial area bordering on most of the Serb villages which had almost 100 percent ethnically pure composition next to the town of Brcko. So the divide would be along the line of the industrial zone towards the centre of town, an ending at river Brka. Another line was supposed to go along Potocari and the local commune of Grtica [phoen], partially encompassing a part of new Brcko, and going along the middle of the main road towards the post building as well as the police station building, ending at Brka river. So it was the whole industrial zone and almost 80 per cent of the town itself. That was their proposal, and the other parties did not wish to discuss that. That's why he issued the ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 103, lines 16 to 19, I think the witness said something different, so if my learned friend can readdress this with the witness so we can have the exact words of the witness in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, the question was did they explain during this meeting which parts of the town the SDS wanted to be part of the Serbian Brcko, and the answer is that based on the maps of the town of Brcko what they wanted to have was most of the industrial area. I will deal with this immediately. Witness, if we were to provide you a map, would you be able to indicated this area?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I think I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we call up 65 ter 3161. And perhaps with the assistance of the usher, the witness could be provided with the magic pen to mark this area on the screen. The map is on the screen, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you see it, Mr. Gasi?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now the usher will provide you a pen. And if you could mark the area that the SDS was proposing to be part of the Serbian municipality of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: It was supposed to start somewhere here, following through here. This would be it. [In English] It would start here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: All the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you mark that area with a number 1, the area that was supposed to be part of the SDS plans. Just so we can differentiate the zones. Just mark a 1 and put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, if we could capture that image. I'd like to ask that the two maps be tendered separately, the one that has the marking and the one that does not have the marking as we will be using the map further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to be -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: My apologies, the clean map will become Exhibit P127, and the map with markings will be Exhibit P128.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be shown 65 ter 267.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gasi, I'm going to show you a newspaper article from the daily newspaper Oslobodjenje. Do you see it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When was the first time you saw this article?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Two days ago. I was shown this article by you in your office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to read the article?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I read it, all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the third paragraph under the section called: SDS Demands Division, do you see the section that talks about the rightful division. It's a paragraph that begins with "Observers from the European Community appealed on the reason ..." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I was just looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you see that section that says according to that rightful division, Serbs would get all economy in Brcko, as well as educational facilities, culture, traffic, PTT, hotel, barracks, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, does that fit with your recollection of the demands of the SDS in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Precisely, yes, you're correct. That's it. It seems that the journalist was well-informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I take you to the second column in B/C/S. And in English, that is the top of the second page. Now when I say second column in B/C/S, it's actually the third column on that page, but it's the second column of the article. Yeah, right there. Maybe a little bit lower as well. Does it deal with the ethnic breakdown in the down and the municipality of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. Muslims, 40 per cent; Serbs, 18.9; Croats, 25; and then there are Yugoslavs and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And does that reflect the ethnic break down prior to the war in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Finally, the last item I'd like to deal with in this article is at the bottom of the second column in B/C/S, and the middle of the second page in English, the issue of the blowing up of the bridge on the 30th of April. And I'd like to you read that section and tell us if it fits with your recollection of the events in 1992.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. Everything in the article is as if the person writing it was on the spot. It happened exactly as described.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours I'm mindful of the time that we must break for the day. So before I move to another topic, if I can ask this article to be admitted and we can resume tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, concerning the proposal to have this admitted, we already have this witness's -- or another witness's statement that was admitted. He discussed the events. This witness did not identify neither the article nor the author, because he saw it only two days ago for the first time. I believe it to be second or third-hand evidence, and, at the same time, we have another witness, witness's statement on the same circumstances. Therefore, I don't think the preconditions are met to have this article admitted. The witness cannot identify it and has no knowledge of it. It was only shown to him two days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, I was about to ask counsel on what basis is this admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a publically available newspaper article that corroborates what this witness said in the Krajisnik case. It corroborates the elements of his evidence that he actually witnessed in 1992, and once again it is a publicly available document that assists him in -- basically corroborating his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But it's -- so far as we know, it's a -- from an unknown source, an anonymous article which is the -- to use your word, is -- adds nothing to what this witness is saying. It merely says the same thing by some unknown, unidentified person. What is the connection?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours, for interrupting. This article comes from a well-known and reputable and newspaper in the region, Oslobodjenje. It has a date and is also authored by the journalist, Mr. Bosanac. Now that, I believe, is sufficient to have -- for the question of admissibility of the document. Now, as to what weight is given later on is another issue, but at this stage we have the title, we have the source, we know which newspaper it comes from, and we an author. And clearly from what the witness says, the author seems to be well-informed or was there during those events. I'm also reminded that newspaper articles are admissible under the jurisprudence of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think [Microphone not activated]. Yes, sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you have something to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of principle I object too. If we open this avenue, then we should be covered with the newspaper articles, various sources, et cetera. We have to keep in accordance with your guidance, really, I would say exact standard which particular potential exhibit must fulfil to be exhibited. As we -- we witnessed -- as we are all witness, this afternoon and this morning, very serious materials related to previous witness where he was the author and go in the core of our case were in accordance with the suggestions of Trial Chamber, I would say assessed in the other way. So I strongly believe that this practice should stop with -- with newspaper articles, et cetera. We know what is in newspapers and we can rebut as many -- as much as possible, if it necessary. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there doesn't seem to be any challenge to the admissibility of the document. It just seems that there is a general rejection of newspaper articles, and Mr. Pantelic is saying that these document have to go to the core of this case. This case -- this newspaper deals with takeover of the municipality of Brcko and deals with the core issues in this case. I don't see what the basis is for --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You can get it from this witness, just simply ask him what was his personal knowledge, and then he can give you his -- I don't have any problem with that. Then he will, as eye-witness, give you a testimony. If you are going along this ways we should be completely blocked with a millions of -- tons of newspapers, articles, and we know all what was the role of media in war, in propaganda, et cetera. So what's the basis for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Accepting the -- as you have kindly alerted me, the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is that the general admissibility of articles of this nature, nevertheless, in terms of the -- what this article says in the context of the witness' testimony, we are of the view that it adds nothing and therefore we aren't going to admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Much obliged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The witness has had the opportunity to read it and comment on it, and his comments are a part of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And it is five minutes -- six minutes past the time of adjournment. So we resume at --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do have a further question, and that's this. We're obviously delayed. Mr. Delic took a lot longer than anticipated. Can I ask what Your Honours would intend to happen if Ms. Hanson does not complete her evidence on Thursday, lunch-time, because we've got two witnesses who are the subject of witness summonses fixed for next week, Tuesday, the 27th, and Thursday, the 29th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we try to, as we often council counsel, not to anticipate. Today is Tuesday afternoon. It's your witness. You will you assess what the situation is at some point on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, do I understand your question to be whether, as it appears, it may be necessary to use the -- that reserved extended sitting on Thursday. Is that what are you asking? Or are you talking about beyond Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about beyond Thursday. Mr. Zecevic estimates his cross-examination will take six to seven hours, and I think Mr. Pantelic is about a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we're in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not exactly Your Honours, no, because we can say well, we're go doing interrupt Ms. Hanson and you may take the view that you don't want her interrupted. So to that extent, what we're simply asking: At the moment we have a witness due to fly in for Monday. We have two unmovable witnesses for Tuesday and Thursday, who are big witnesses on the face of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Why don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the event, which we anticipate is likely, that Ms. Hanson will not finish testifying, even if you were to sit extended on Thursday but would go into Monday, whether you would object, because you are the -- the Judges who are moving this case on, if we have a then a gap until the Tuesday witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We would certainly avoid having gaps, and we are not going to tell you in which order you must bring your witnesses. If you advise the Chamber that we can avoid gaps by interrupting Mrs. Hanson and then taking the two other witnesses in between and then call her back, or if you want to use Mrs. Hanson to fill out any further gaps that may arise later on, then I think it's basically for the Defence to indicate their position about this, whether they would accept having interrupted testimonies from Mrs. Hanson. The Chamber, as such, does not oppose that. We are only interested in moving ahead and avoiding gaps. So in the end I think if the Defence can live with it, then that's fine with us. I don't know if have you a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not at the moment, Your Honour. We have to think about it because it opens up quite a few questions. Thank you very much. But I will inform Ms. Korner immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
